newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. tobacco deal is unlikely precedent for France.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco deal is unlikely precedent for France.

text.p: French anti-tobacco activists hailed a landmark accord between U.S. authorities and cigarette companies, but the tobacco industry and financial analysts said such a settlement was unlikely in France.

Shares in tobacco firm Seita, which makes pungent Gauloises and Gitanes cigarettes, initially dropped on Monday on news that U.S. cigarette makers had agreed to pay out $368.5 billion over 25 years for damages and anti-smoking campaigns.
But the stock recovered to close with a small 0.26 percent gain at 190.50 francs after share analysts judged the U.S. deal was unlikely to spur action against European tobacco groups.
"It's wrong to see a settlement in the States as an opportunity to pursue tobacco companies in other countries," one analyst said.
"There are big differences in legal structure that make it harder for plaintiffs to sue the tobacco industry elsewhere."
The U.S. settlement "will have a limited impact on European tobacco companies", said another specialist, Emilio Alvarez at Morgan Stanley.
The concept of product liability is not as developed in Europe as it is in the United States, and the European tobacco industry already contributes more to public revenue, he said.
Tax on cigarettes in most of western Europe is more than twice the average U.S. rate of just over 30 percent.
A spokeswoman for Seita said taxes account for 76 percent of the price of a packet of cigarettes in France.
Some U.S. advertising methods that would be banned under the settlement have been illegal in France for years.

"Advertising using images like the Marlboro Man cowboy and Joe Camel has been banned since 1976 and all cigarette advertising has been prohibited since 1991," the spokeswoman said. "We operate in a very strictly regulated environment."
The 1991 law also barred the broadcasting of sports events featuring prominent tobacco advertising.
Despite the higher tax and stricter laws against cigarette advertising, smoking is far more prevalent in France, due in part to lagging demographic trends.
French women, for instance, did not take up the habit in big numbers until the 1970s, according to the national committee against smoking.
About 37 percent of French adults smoke, but among teenagers the proportion is an alarming 50 percent, it said, compared with 25 percent of U.S. adults and 35 percent of high school pupils.
"This settlement is a start, and other governments will have to take note," said Philippe Boucher, director of the committee. "The threat of lawsuits is here, too."

A French court this year threw out a lawsuit alleging that a victim had died due to "passive smoking" at the workplace. Two other lawsuits are pending against Seita, one filed by a smoker and another by the relatives of a deceased smoker.

Last month a court fined SNCF state railways for failing to enforce a ban on smoking in the Gare de Lyon in Paris. The 1991 ban is widely ignored in restaurants and offices, but largely respected in the Paris Metro underground railway.
